title: Training Language Model Agents to Find Vulnerabilities with CTF-Dojo
one_liner: Train security-oriented agents inside runnable challenge environments where success and failure can be checked directly by execution.
lead: Security tasks are hard to train from text alone because the agent must try commands, inspect outputs, and see whether an exploit attempt actually works. This paper builds a large collection of reproducible Capture-The-Flag challenge environments and uses verified execution traces to train agents. The main idea is simple: if the environment can confirm whether a step worked, training gets a clearer signal because success is grounded in actual behavior rather than guesswork.

problem.h2: Why training security agents is harder than training from static text
paras: Finding a software weakness is an interactive task. The agent has to inspect files, run commands, test hypotheses, and revise its plan after seeing the machine's response. Static text examples do not capture that loop well because the key signal comes from what happens when the agent acts.

Good training environments are scarce. Many security setups take expert time to configure, and small ad hoc setups are hard to reproduce. That makes it difficult to scale agent training or compare methods fairly because each team ends up working with a different and often unstable setup.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build a large reproducible collection of runnable security challenges and train from execution-verified traces so that the agent learns from outcomes the environment can check directly.

steps.text: Provide hundreds of containerized security challenges so that training runs in reproducible environments.
Use CTF-Forge to turn public challenge artifacts into runnable setups because manual configuration does not scale.
Keep traces whose steps can be checked by execution so that the training signal reflects actual success.

steps.b: Train the agent on those traces
steps.text: Update the model using verified problem-solving behavior because grounded traces connect actions to consequences.
Measure pass rates on separate benchmarks so that the benefit transfers beyond the training set.

paras: The paper changes the source of supervision for security agents. Instead of relying mostly on text descriptions of good behavior, it draws supervision from live environments that can accept or reject what the agent actually did.
object.object: the training signal used to teach a security-focused agent

hidden.name: which action sequence will expose the weakness in the current environment
paras: The central hidden quantity is the useful path through the challenge environment. At the start, the agent does not know which commands, files, or tests will reveal the weakness.

It can only discover that path by acting and reading the environment's response. That matters because wrong early moves can waste time, while a good probe can reveal the structure of the challenge and point toward a working exploit path.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark pieces of environment feedback that can sharply narrow the search for a working exploit path.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the sequence of actions that will actually break the challenge in the live environment.
The dataset and training setup matter because they let the agent search for that path under direct executable feedback.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: executable feedback ties actions to truth
paras: A text-only training example can tell the agent that a certain exploit plan is good, yet it does not show whether each step still works in a live environment. Security work depends heavily on that distinction because small command errors or wrong assumptions break the whole attempt.

CTF-Dojo closes that gap by making the environment itself part of the supervision loop. When the agent runs a command, the machine answers. When the exploit works, the setup confirms it. That grounded loop gives cleaner credit to the steps that actually caused success, so training can favor behavior that survives execution.

stages.s: Runnable security challenge in a reproducible container
Agent explores with commands and tests
Environment verifies whether the steps worked
Training reinforces verified successful traces because the machine checked them
An agent with higher challenge-solving success because it learned from checked execution

math.h2: Prefer trajectories whose success is verified by execution
math.words: A simple summary is to score each candidate trajectory by whether it solves the challenge and by how much of the path is confirmed through execution. Training prefers traces with higher grounded score.
symbols: overall training value of one challenge-solving path
how much the path contributes to solving the challenge
how much of the path is directly confirmed by runnable feedback
weight on the execution-verified part of the score

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Path A proposes an exploit but never confirms it inside the environment.
Its solve value is 4 and its verify value is 0, so with beta equal to 1 the total score is 4.
Path B reaches the same idea and then confirms it with working commands.
Its solve value is 4 and its verify value is 3, so the total score is 7.
Training prefers Path B because execution checked the key steps.

math.note: The paper uses a fuller training recipe, but this score captures the central point that executable confirmation improves the learning signal because the environment verifies whether the chosen actions actually worked.

charts.title: Strong text-based or weaker-grounded baselines
charts.note: Baselines lag because they have less grounded practice inside checked environments.

charts.title: CTF-Dojo-trained agent
charts.note: The paper reports absolute gains and stronger open-weight results because verified execution traces teach the agent which actions truly work.

items.b: Challenge environments may still differ from live systems.
items.html: A containerized exercise is more controlled than a messy production network, so transfer can weaken when real conditions add noise or hidden dependencies.

items.b: Verified traces can still be narrow.
items.html: If most training traces solve similar classes of challenge, the agent may overfit to those routines because it sees fewer varied attack patterns.

items.b: Automation can reproduce setup mistakes at scale.
items.html: If the pipeline builds a flawed environment, that flaw can spread into many tasks because the automated process repeats it consistently.
The framework is useful because it gives agents a place to learn from executable truth rather than from unsupported text-only claims.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build five small security tasks inside containers, such as file disclosure, weak permissions, and simple service misuse. Compare an agent trained on written solutions alone against an agent trained on execution-verified traces from the same style of environment.

The demo should log command success, discovered clues, and final challenge completion. It should show that the execution-trained agent improves because it learns which trial actions expose real structure in the environment and which ones fail immediately.
demo.metric_eq: grounded_gain = pass_rate_dojo - pass_rate_text_only ; verified_step_share = verified_steps / total_steps
demo.closing: The point is to show that live checked environments can provide a cleaner teacher for security agents.
